Catalán’s multiparametric analysis. As shown in Fig. 5, in a similar 
frame to that reported for 2 the lowest-energy electronic transition 
of dye 3 (similar to 4–6, see Supplementary Material) involves a 
clear intramolecular phenolate-to-nitroaryl charge transfer, with the 
HOMO localized in the donor phenolate and the LUMO centered on the 
nitroaryl acceptor. This redistribution of the electron density implies a 
more localized and hydrogen-bond-accessible ground state, in contrast 
to a more charge-separated, polarizable excited state.
The TDDFT calculations predict two low-lying electronic transitions 
with a distinct character. The higher-energy transition corresponds to a 
localized 𝜋–𝜋∗ excitation, assigned to the high-energy absorption band 
observed in the UV–Vis spectra (Fig. 3), which shows only weak solva-
tochromic sensitivity. The calculated energy for this transition (84.79 
kcal mol−1) is in reasonable agreement with the experimental value 
(77.48 kcal mol−1), supporting its assignment. In contrast, the lower-
energy transition that dominates the visible region corresponds to 
an intramolecular charge-transfer (ICT) excitation from the phenolate 
donor to the nitroaryl acceptor.
For this ICT band, the dominance of SA in the negative solva-
tochromic region reflects preferential ground-state stabilization via 
hydrogen-bond donation to the phenolate moiety, as revealed by the 
Catalán analysis. Upon excitation, electron density shifts towards the 
nitroaryl unit, reducing the relevance of hydrogen bonding and in-
creasing the sensitivity of the excited state to nonspecific solvent inter-
actions. Consequently, the positive solvatochromic region is governed 
by a cooperative contribution of SP, SdP, and SB, with polarizability 
(SP) as the leading factor, consistent with stabilization of a delocalized 
and highly polarizable ICT excited state. The close agreement between 
experimental transition energies (57.18 kcal mol−1) and calculated en-
ergies (59.44 kcal mol−1) for this band further validates the electronic 
assignment and provides a unified TDDFT–Catalán interpretation of 
inverted solvatochromic behavior.
3. Conclusions
In this work, we show how the 𝜋-bridge enables the modulation 
of inverted solvatochromism in phenolate–nitroaryl push–𝜋–pull chro-
mophores. Both the spatial arrangement of the aromatic spacer and 
the electronic characteristics of the nitroaryl acceptor exert a decisive 
influence on the solvatochromic behavior, leading to shifts in the 
solvatochromic inversion point (SIP) and alterations in solvent sensi-
tivity. Whereas the reference dye exhibits inversion only at relatively 
high solvent polarities, structural reorganization in the newly designed 
derivatives shifts the inversion towards lower polarity domains and 
produces distinct sensitivity profiles.
Multiparametric regression analysis employing Catalán’s solvent 
scales reveals a distinct mechanistic bifurcation underlying the two 
branches of the inverted solvatochromic response: negative solva-
tochromism is dictated exclusively by the hydrogen-bond donor ca-
pacity of the medium, while positive solvatochromism originates from 
a cooperative interplay between solvent polarizability, dipolarity, and 
basicity, with polarizability emerging as the predominant determinant. 
Time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) calculations corrob-
orate that the lowest-energy absorption band arises from a phenolate-
to-nitroaryl intramolecular charge-transfer transition, yielding a highly 
polarizable excited state whose differential stabilization accounts for 
the observed solvent-dependent behavior. Collectively, these findings 
establish a unified structure–solvent–electronic correlation framework 
and identify 𝜋-bridge engineering as a powerful design strategy to 
modulate the properties of solvent-responsive chromophores.

tioned between the hydrophilic fluorine-substituted, bis-triazole anti­
fungal agent fluconazole (logP of 0.5) and the lipophilic miconazole 
(logP of 6.1).
In the context of phospholipid binding (CHIIAM), the scenario is 
somewhat distinct, as both sulfonamides exhibit a higher affinity for 
phospholipids than reference antifungal drugs, except miconazole. 
Notably, the structures under examination did not exceed the 50 CHIIAM 
threshold, which indicates non-specific binding to phospholipids and 
suggests a potential risk of phospholipidosis [81].
The final endpoint assessed through chromatography was the bind­
ing to HSA, constituting the predominant plasma protein, representing 
approximately 70 % of the total plasma protein fraction. The high af­
finity for plasma proteins can raise safety concerns, such as reduced 
clearance, limited brain penetration, and diminished pharmacological 
efficacy, since only unbound molecules can interact with their intended 
targets [47]. Conversely, weak protein binding minimizes a drug's effect 
duration and accelerates its elimination [81]. As is typical for this class 
of chemicals, the newly synthesised sulphonamide derivatives exhibited 
a strong affinity for HSA. However, their binding levels must remain at 
an acceptable level, which is lower than that of the reference set of 
marketed drugs like diclofenac.
Notably, the results obtained by chromatography and the shake-flask 
method remain consistent, +2.09 for SNaft and +1.93 for SAntr, they 
indicate the hydrophilic-hydrophobic nature of the compounds, which 
also translates into the other experiments performed (the data con­
cerning the experiment are contained in Table S7 and in Fig. S9-S12). 
These properties of the compound may promote its bioavailability and 
penetration through phospholipid cell membranes, which is a key factor 
determining its pharmacological activity. The ability to effectively cross 
cell membranes increases the likelihood of achieving adequate concen­
trations within the cell and effectively interacting with target molecular 
structures.
Regarding the equilibrium structures of the studied compounds, the 
CSNC dihedral angle (as defined in Fig. 7) scans suggest the existence of 
three minima (Fig. 8) for both SNaft and SAntr regardless of ionization 
state. Geometrically, two of these minima adopt a V-like conformation 
with CSNC dihedral angle value close to ±50 degrees [33,70]. The 
remaining minimum is Z-Shaped with a value of the corresponding 
dihedral angle at about 180 degrees. Analysis of the chart reveals that 
the V-like structures are nearly equivalent in energy, whereas the Z 
conformer is energetically less favorable. The neutral systems' differ­
ences are most pronounced, amounting to 3.05 and 3.03 kcal/mol for 
SNaft and SAntr, respectively. These differences mainly originate from 
intramolecular hydrogen bonds in the V-shaped conformers, which are 
discussed in detail in the following sections of this manuscript.
The first thing that stands out from the analyses of the graphs shown 
in Fig. 9 is that the plots calculated for protonated systems differ 
significantly from those obtained for neutral and deprotonated systems. 
Namely, for BH2
+, the barriers between V(+)⇌V(-) and V⇌Z transitions 
are almost alike and close to 2 kcal/mol. Additionally, the Z conformers 
are only circa 0.5 kcal/mol higher in energy than their V-shaped 
counterparts. Together, these two observations indicate that in a 
strongly acidic environment, SNaft and SAntr readily adopt all three 
conformations and can freely isomerize.
On the other hand, the plots obtained for deprotonated and neutral 
forms of SNaft and SAntr are alike. Specifically, the V(+)⇌V(-) transi­
tion proceeds over a 6-7 kcal/mol barrier. In contrast, the V(+)⇌Z and V 
(-)⇌Z transition energy barriers are equal to about 4.20 kcal/mol. 
Additionally, when going from SNaft to SAntr, the V(+)⇌V(-) trans­
formation barrier for the B- decreases by circa 0.9 kcal/mol, placing it 
below the barrier calculated for BH. A similar trend is observed for 
lower-barrier transitions associated with V(+)⇌Z and V(-)⇌Z. These 
observations, together with the relative energies of conformers, imply 
that for SNaft and SAntr in both BH and B-forms, the V-like conformers 
are favorable. At the same time, the V⇌Z interconversions are more 
feasible than the V(+)⇌V(-) ones.
Polarity is of utmost importance when describing potential drugs, as 
it allows one to assess the dissolution processes in gastrointestinal fluids 
and passing through cell membranes. Thus, in this paper, polarity was 
examined from multiple perspectives by assessing: dipole moment, polar 
surface area, logP, and logD values (vide Table 4). All parameters used to 
evaluate the tested systems' polarity level indicate a significant value of 
this quantity. Initially, it seems quite unexpected that sulfonamides 
substituted with non-polar systems such as naphthalene or anthracene 
are significantly polar, especially regarding V-shaped systems. As shown 
in Fig. S13 using SNaft-V(+)as an example, the dipole moment vector is 
located in a way that makes the sulfonamide group the negative end of 
the vector (vertex of the V), whereas the aromatic rings of both PAH and 
sulfonanilide part constitute a positive end of the dipole moment vector 
(arms of the V). Analogous sulfanilamide derivatives based on thiazolo 
[4,5-d]pyrimidine moiety investigated as potential Carbonic Anhy­
drase II (CA II) and Dickkopf-1 (DKK1) inhibitors were found to have a 
dipole moment higher than 13D in most cases, regardless of the basis set 
used during the calculations [82].
Similar to the dipole moment, polar surface values also reflect sig­
nificant polarity of studied systems, as for all studied compounds, it was 
calculated to account for 67-69 % of the total surface area. This trans­
lates to a polar surface area above 210 Å2 for both studied systems in 
each conformation. As such, they fail to obey Veber’s rule, which states 
that only compounds with a polar surface area equal to or less than 140 
Å2 are likely to have significant oral bioavailability [83]. In like manner, 
log P values calculated for each studied conformer are negative, indi­
cating hydrophilicity. With the value of -0.632, SAntr-Z is the least hy­
drophilic outlier here. The values of logP calculated for the remaining 
conformers fall into the -1.200 to -1.500 range. The lipophilicity order 
may thus look as follows: SAntr-V(+) ≈SNaft-V(–) ≈SNaft-Z < SNaft-V 
(+) < SAntr-V(–) < SAntr-Z. Two reasons exist for the differences be­
tween logP values determined experimentally and by computational 
methods. First, naphthalene and anthracene moieties may favor π–π 
stacking while in solution, creating corresponding dimers or even olig­
omers. This can significantly increase partitioning, making the experi­
mental values more lipophilic than the monomer-based calculations. 
Second, the calculations are based on a single structure within a solvent 
approximated by a continuum, thus missing possible conformers and 
protomer populations present during experimental measurements.
The graph presenting the logD(pH) profile for all conformers is 
shown in Fig. 9. The first thing that comes to mind while analyzing the 
presented plots is that logD values are always negative, regardless of the 
pH value or compound/conformer considered. The steep rise in logD 
values from 0 to 5 corresponds to crossing the pKa1 value of 4.3-4.7. 
Chemically, protonation (BH2+ to neutral (BH)) occurs in this range. 
These results suggest that at gastric pH (1-2), all conformers are over 99 
% protonated. A flat plateau between pH of circa 5.5 and 11 corresponds 
to the range within which 98-100 % are neutral, corresponding to blood, 
cytosol, and intestinal fluid environments. The ordering of the plateau 
reflects the logP order mentioned in the previous paragraph. The 
downturn occurs at pH values close to 12. It corresponds to the

One way to decrease their polarity, and thus increase hydrophobic­
ity, is to introduce the polar substituent into the PAH ring, preferably at 
the end opposite to the sulfonamide group. Preliminary calculations 
show that the mono-chloro-substituted (in the 6th position) derivatives 
of the studied compounds have a dipole moment lower by circa two 
units.
The parameters characterizing hydrogen bonds within V-shaped 
conformers of SNaft and SAntr are collected in Table S7. The values of 
H/ρ and |V|/G were calculated to 0.17 and 0.79, respectively, for each of 
the (PAH)-C-H•••O hydrogen bonds investigated. This type of non- 
covalent interaction is known to have similar properties to regular 
hydrogen bonds, although their energies are typically in the 0.5–2.5 
kcal/mol range [84]. H/ρ and |V|/G values indicate that the interaction 
is dominated by electrostatic or dispersion contributions rather than 
electron sharing. Additionally, the studied non-covalent interactions 
exhibit closed-shell character and are relatively weak. These findings are 
further confirmed by hydrogen bond energies calculated with Espinosa’s 
method, as the values calculated for all studied systems are within the 
2.40-2.55 kcal/mol range. The presence of those non-covalent in­
teractions, and their absence in the protonated counterparts, indicates 
that rotation of PAH along the C-N axis may be slightly hindered in the 
case of the former. Also, by hiding the otherwise highly electronegative 
oxygen inside the molecule, the discussed H-bond effectively lowers the 
resulting polarity, thereby increasing passive membrane permeability. 
This effect is mirrored in the polarity assessments.
The in vitro biological activity of the synthesized compounds SNaft 
and SAntr was evaluated across a panel of human cancer cell lines, 
bacterial, and fungal strains. A summary of the IC₅₀ and MIC₅₀ values is 
presented in Table 5. Cytotoxicity assays revealed that SNaft exhibited 
moderate antiproliferative activity, particularly against the A-549 non- 
small cell lung cancer line (IC₅₀ = 30.17 ± 4.77 µM). Comparable, yet 
weaker effects were observed in NALM-6 (42.78 ± 2.92 µM) and MCF-7 
(50.06 ± 6.17 µM) cells, while HCT-116 cells displayed lower sensitivity 
(78.81 ± 8.74 µM). In contrast, SAntr did not demonstrate cytotoxic 
effects in any of the tested cancer lines at concentrations up to 100 µM. 
Both compounds were inactive against the non-tumorigenic HEK-293 
cell line, indicating a favorable selectivity profile. Cisplatin, used as a 
reference agent, exhibited expected potent cytotoxicity in all cancer 
models, with the lowest IC₅₀ recorded for NALM-6 (0.83 ± 0.15 µM), but 
also affected nonmalignant cells (IC₅₀ = 30.59 ± 20.7 µM) [84–87] .

We evaluated μ, m, and θ for (S)-di-ClPDI-Ph in its
HOMO→LUMO and HOMO→LUMO + 1 transitions
(Tables S2–S6). While the μ and m of the two fragments
are initially perpendicular to each other, the gabs values
of monomer (S)-ClPDI-Ph are nearly negligible, which is
consistent with experimental results. Nevertheless, upon
fusion of the two fragments, the resulting µsum and msum
become nearly collinear (Figure 1g; Figures S12 and S13).
Speciﬁcally, for both Fragment A and Fragment B in the
HOMO→LUMO transition, m is nearly perpendicular to μ.
However, when these fragments are fused into the dimer
(S)-di-ClPDI-Ph, msum becomes nearly collinear with µsum,
enhancing the dot product of µsum and msum and resulting
in high |gabs| values. Similarly, in the HOMO→LUMO + 1
transition, after fusing Fragment A and Fragment B, the
relative orientation of m and μ changes from perpendicular
to nearly collinear, also increasing the |gabs| values. The
π-extended helitwistacene framework, realized through the
CπE strategy, therefore enforces optimal transition dipole
alignment, simultaneously preserving and amplifying helicity
while extending conjugation. This synergy yields high |gabs|
values and broad spectral response—deﬁning the hallmark of
the CπE design concept.

molecules, motivating the investigation of the morphology
and chiroptical properties of the CπE-engineered materials
in the single-crystal state. Single crystals of (R)- and (S)-di-
ClPDI-Ph were obtained at room temperature via the slow
diffusion of methanol into a toluene solution. Experimental
details and crystallization procedures are provided in the

planarity and helicity are harmonized within a single π-

Device Fabrication and Optoelectronic Performance
To
evaluate
the
optoelectronic
performance
and
CPL
detection capabilities of the π-extended helitwistacene,
two-terminal Ag/(S/R)-di-ClPDI-Ph/Ag photodetectors were
fabricated (Figure 3a). Beneﬁting from the CπE-induced π-
extension and optimized crystal packing, the (S)-di-ClPDI-Ph
device exhibited strong and broadband photoresponse across
the UV–visible range (365–690 nm; Figure 3b). The current–
voltage (I–V) characteristics measured in the dark and
under monochromatic illumination (Figure 3c; Figure S19)
demonstrate pronounced photocurrent generation, even at
low irradiance levels. Key performance metrics extracted
from these measurements (Figure 3d; Figure S20) reveal
outstanding device performance, with maximum external
quantum efﬁciency (EQE), R, and D* values of 1780.4%, 9.1
A W−1, and 4.8 × 1012 Jones, respectively (Table S8). These
values exceed those of most previously reported intrinsic
chiral small-molecule CPL detectors by one to two orders of
magnitude in both R and D* (Table S9).

To assess the antiosteoporosis activity of 1−5, the receptor
activator of nuclear factor κB ligand (RANKL) -induced
RAW264.7 cell was employed. As shown in Figure 3A,B, the
increased cell volume and tartrate resistant acid phosphatase

comparison with the MOD group, 1, 4 and 5 effectively
inhibited the osteoclast differentiation and decreased the
number of osteoclasts. The results indicated that 1, 4 and 5
exhibit antiosteoporosis activity. To further evaluate the
antiosteoporosis activity in vivo, we established a dexametha-

revealed that the staining area was significantly reduced in MOD
group, which compared with the control (CON) group, and
treatment with 1, 4, and 5 significantly restored the staining area
(Figure 3C,D). The above results demonstrated the anti-
osteoporosis efficacy of 1, 4, and 5 in vitro and in vivo.
Additionally, as shown in Figure S39, none of the compounds 1,
4, and 5 tested displayed cytotoxicity at a concentration of 100
μM. In contrast, 2 exhibited no antiosteoporosis activity,
suggesting that the hydroxyl group at C-7″ may be crucial.
When the C-7″ position was oxygen-methylated, the Δ10 double
bond appeared somewhat unnecessary for activity. Antiosteopo-
rosis activity was restored only when the Δ10 double bond was
reduced, which also explains why 2 and 3 lack activity, while 4
remains active.
In summary, four novel pyrazines and one related biosynthetic
analog from Alternaria sp. HJT-Y7. The structures and absolute
configurations of these compounds were determined through a
combination of NMR, HRESIMS, and ECD spectroscopic data.
Notably, three of them (1, 4, and 5) suppressed osteoclast
differentiation in RANKL-induced RAW264.7 cells and
significantly enhanced bone mineralization in a dexametha-
sone-induced zebrafish model of osteoporosis, highlighting its
potential as a promising lead for osteolytic disease treatment.
These findings expand the chemical and bioactive diversity of
pyrazines, providing a foundation for their further investigation
as potential therapeutic agents for osteoporosis and for the
exploration of their biosynthetic pathways.
■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
General Experimental Procedures
Optical rotations were determined using a Rudolph Autopol IV
polarimeter (Rudolph Research Analytical, Flanders, NJ, USA) at 20
°C. Ultraviolet (UV) spectra were recorded on a Techcomp UV2600
spectrophotometer (Techcomp Group, Beijing, China). IR spectrum
was recorded on a Thermo Scientific Nicolete iS20 Fourier transform
infrared (FT-IR) spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA,
USA). High-resolution electrospray ionization mass spectra (HRE-
SIMS) were acquired on an AB Sciex Triple TOF 4600 system (AB
SCIEX, Framingham, MA, USA). Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)
spectra, including 1H, 13C, and 2D experiments, were recorded on a
Bruker Avance II 500 MHz spectrometer (Bruker, Karlsruhe,
Germany). Chemical shifts (δ) are reported in ppm, with coupling
constants (J) expressed in Hz, and were referenced to the residual
solvent signal of DMSO-d6. Circular dichroism (CD) spectra were
measured using a Jasco J-810−150S spectropolarimeter (JASCO
Corporation, Tokyo, Japan). Semipreparative high-performance liquid
chromatography (HPLC) was carried out on Agilent 1260 Infinity
(Agilent Technologies Inc., Santa Clara, CA, USA) and Shimadzu LC-
20AR (Shimadzu Corporation, Kyoto, Japan) systems equipped with a
Welch Ultimate XB-C18 column (250 mm × 10.0 mm, 5 μm). For
column chromatography (CC), silica gel (100−200 and 200−300
mesh; Qingdao Marine Chemical Co., Ltd., Qingdao, China) and
Sephadex LH-20 (GE Healthcare Bio-Sciences AB, Uppsala, Sweden)
were employed. Analytical and preparative thin-layer chromatography
(TLC) was performed on precoated silica gel GF254 plates (Qingdao
Marine Chemistry Co., Ltd., Qingdao, China).
Fungal Strain and Fermentation
The fungal strain HJT-Y7 was obtained from the leaves of R. tibetica.
Based on sequence analysis of the ITS1−5.8S−ITS2 region of the
rDNA (GenBank accession number: PP941786), the isolate was
identified as Alternaria sp. The strain has been deposited at the Institute
of Microbiology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CGMCC No. 40166),
and a voucher specimen is maintained at the College of Life and Health,
Dalian University, Dalian, China.
For cultivation, the fungus was initially grown on potato dextrose
agar (PDA; potato starch 4 g/L, dextrose 20 g/L, agar 15 g/L) plates at
28 °C for 5 days. The resulting mycelial mats were cut into small
fragments and transferred into 250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks containing
100 mL of potato dextrose broth (PDB; potato starch 4 g/L, dextrose
20 g/L). The cultures were incubated on a rotary shaker (120 rpm) at
28 °C for 3 days to prepare the seed inoculum. Large-scale fermentation
was subsequently carried out in one hundred 500 mL Erlenmeyer flasks,
each containing 80 g of rice and 110 mL of distilled water, and
incubated at 28 °C under static conditions for 40 days.
Extraction and Isolation
The cultures were extracted with MeOH, and the extract solution was
evaporated to yield a total of 207 g of crude extract. The extract was
subjected to column chromatography (CC) over silica gel (CH2Cl2/
MeOH, v/v, 100:0 →0:100) to afford 11 fractions (Fr.1−Fr.11). Fr.8
was further separated by CC on silica gel (PE/EtOAc, v/v, 100:0 →
0:100) to yield 22 subfractions. Subfraction Fr.8.11 was purified by
reversed-phase HPLC (CH3CN/H2O, 48:52, 3 mL/min) to obtain 2
(36.8 mg, tR = 26.0 min) and 3 (2.5 mg, tR = 17.0 min). Subfraction
Fr.8.12 was applied to reversed-phase HPLC (MeOH/H2O, 63:37, 3
mL/min) to afford 4 (4.5 mg, tR = 23.8 min). Subfraction Fr.8.14 was
purified via reversed-phase HPLC (MeOH/H2O, 60:40, 3 mL/min) to
give 1 (21.8 mg, tR = 36.0 min). Subfraction Fr.8.22 was separated by
reversed-phase HPLC (MeOH/H2O, 33:67, 3 mL/min) to yield 5 (6.5
mg, tR = 7.1 min).

1. Experimental Methods
1.1 Synthesis of Chiral PDIs and Crystal Growth
(S)- and (R)-1-Phenylethylamine were purchased from Adamas without further
purification. For the synthesis of (S/R)-ClPDI-Ph, 1,6,7,12-Tetrachloroperylene

class TaskRepository:
    """Validated index keyed by ``(task_type, paper_id)``."""

    def __init__(self, roots: Iterable[str | Path] | None = None):
        self.roots = tuple(
            dict.fromkeys(Path(root).expanduser().resolve() for root in (roots or TASK_ROOTS))
        )
        self._index = self._build_index()

    @classmethod
    def from_final(
        cls, task_root: str | Path, *, approved_tasks: Iterable[tuple[str, str]]
    ) -> "TaskRepository":
        """Opt-in final-only loading; explicit (mode, paper_id) approval is required.

        This does not declare packages scientifically publishable or change default
        canonical discovery. Callers must approve the audited version, not all
        packages merely because they reside in a final directory.
        """
        import re

        root = Path(task_root).expanduser().resolve()
        directories = []
        seen = set()
        for mode, paper_id in approved_tasks:
            if mode not in {"autonomous_research", "paper_reproduction"}:
                raise InvalidTaskPackageError(f"invalid_final_mode:{mode}")
            if not re.fullmatch(r"paper_[A-Za-z0-9]+", paper_id):
                raise InvalidTaskPackageError(f"invalid_final_paper_id:{paper_id}")
            if (mode, paper_id) in seen:
                raise DuplicateTaskError(f"duplicate_final_approval:{mode}:{paper_id}")
            seen.add((mode, paper_id))
            directory = root / f"final_verified_{mode}" / paper_id
            if directory.parent.is_symlink() or directory.is_symlink() or not directory.is_dir():
                raise InvalidTaskPackageError(f"invalid_final_directory:{directory}")
            directories.append(directory)
        repository = cls.__new__(cls)
        repository.roots = (root,)
        repository._approved_final_directories = tuple(directories)
        repository._index = repository._build_index()
        return repository

    def _candidate_directories(self) -> list[Path]:
        if hasattr(self, "_approved_final_directories"):
            return list(self._approved_final_directories)
        candidates: list[Path] = []
        for root in self.roots:
            if not root.exists():
                continue
            if root.is_symlink():
                raise InvalidTaskPackageError(f"task_root_is_symlink:{root}")
            for task_type in TASK_TYPES:
                mode_root = root / task_type
                if not mode_root.is_dir():
                    continue
                candidates.extend(
                    path.resolve()
                    for path in sorted(mode_root.iterdir())
                    if path.is_dir() and not path.is_symlink()
                )
        return candidates

    def _build_index(self) -> dict[tuple[str, str], TaskPackage]:
        index: dict[tuple[str, str], TaskPackage] = {}
        paper_modes: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
        for directory in self._candidate_directories():
            validation = validate_task_package(directory)
            if validation.status != "passed":
                raise InvalidTaskPackageError(
                    f"invalid_task_package:{directory}:{';'.join(validation.findings)}"
                )
            info = TaskInfo.model_validate(_read_json(directory / "task_info.json"))
            manifest = _read_json(directory / "package_manifest.json")
            package = TaskPackage(
                paper_id=info.paper_id,
                task_type=info.task_type,
                directory=directory,
                category=info.category,
                difficulty=info.difficulty,
                difficulty_reasons=tuple(info.difficulty_reasons),
                package_content_sha256=str(manifest["package_content_sha256"]),
            )
            if package.key in index:
                previous = index[package.key]
                raise DuplicateTaskError(
                    f"duplicate_task:{package.task_type}:{package.paper_id}:"
                    f"{previous.directory}:{package.directory}"
                )
            index[package.key] = package
            paper_modes.setdefault(package.paper_id, set()).add(package.task_type)
        for paper_id, modes in paper_modes.items():
            if "experiment_validation" in modes and modes & {
                "autonomous_research", "paper_reproduction"
            }:
                raise InvalidTaskPackageError(f"mixed_paper_mode_set:{paper_id}")
        return index

def package_payload_entries(root: str | Path) -> list[ManifestEntry]:
    root = Path(root).resolve()
    entries: list[ManifestEntry] = []
    for path in sorted(root.rglob("*")):
        if path.is_symlink():
            raise ValueError(f"symlink is forbidden: {path.relative_to(root)}")
        if not path.is_file() or path.name == "package_manifest.json":
            continue
        relative = path.relative_to(root).as_posix()
        digest = hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()
        entries.append(
            ManifestEntry(
                path=relative,
                size=path.stat().st_size,
                sha256=digest,
                visibility=_visibility(relative),
            )
        )
    return entries

    typ=s.get('type','object' if 'properties' in s else 'string')

"""Transport contract for current ResearchChemBench task packages.

The contract checks identity, paths, visibility, evaluator completeness and
submission binding.  It deliberately does not judge whether an authored
tolerance or scientific conclusion is optimal.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import json
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath
from typing import Any, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, field_validator, model_validator


TASK_TYPES = (
    "autonomous_research",
    "paper_reproduction",
    "experiment_validation",
)
EVALUATION_FILES = (
    "reference_key_points.json",
    "reference_conclusions.json",
    "scoring_rules.json",
    "evidence_map.json",
    "critical_failures.json",
)
RULE_TYPES = {"numeric", "ordering", "condition", "semantic"}
_PAPER_ID = re.compile(r"paper_[A-Za-z0-9]+\Z")
_PLACEHOLDERS = {"todo", "tbd", "placeholder", "fill me", "fill_me", "fill-me"}


def _safe_path(value: str) -> str:
    if not isinstance(value, str) or not value or "\\" in value or "\x00" in value:
        raise ValueError("path must be a non-empty relative POSIX path")
    path = PurePosixPath(value)
    if path.is_absolute() or any(part in {"", ".", ".."} for part in path.parts):
        raise ValueError("path must be a safe relative POSIX path")
    return path.as_posix()


def _json_object(path: Path) -> dict[str, Any]:
    value = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    if not isinstance(value, dict):
        raise ValueError(f"expected JSON object: {path}")
    return value


def _has_value(value: Any) -> bool:
    if value is None:
        return False
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return bool(value.strip()) and value.strip().casefold() not in _PLACEHOLDERS
    if isinstance(value, (list, dict)):
        return bool(value)
    return True


class StrictModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")


class DataDescription(StrictModel):
    path: str
    description: str

    @field_validator("path")
    @classmethod
    def data_path(cls, value: str) -> str:
        value = _safe_path(value)
        if value != "data" and not value.startswith("data/"):
            raise ValueError("data paths must be rooted below data/")
        return value


class RequiredDeliverable(StrictModel):
    path: str
    description: str

    @field_validator("path")
    @classmethod
    def deliverable_path(cls, value: str) -> str:
        return _safe_path(value)


class PaperSummary(StrictModel):
    title: str = ""
    doi: str = ""
    journal: str = ""
    publication_date: str = ""


class TaskInfo(StrictModel):
    paper_id: str
    task_type: Literal[
        "autonomous_research", "paper_reproduction", "experiment_validation"
    ]
    title: str
    category: str
    difficulty: Literal["easy", "medium", "hard"]
    difficulty_reasons: list[str]
    paper: PaperSummary = Field(default_factory=PaperSummary)
    data: list[DataDescription]
    required_deliverables: list[RequiredDeliverable]

    @field_validator("paper_id")
    @classmethod
    def valid_paper_id(cls, value: str) -> str:
        if not _PAPER_ID.fullmatch(value):
            raise ValueError("paper_id must use paper_<alphanumeric>")
        return value

    @field_validator("title", "category")
    @classmethod
    def nonempty(cls, value: str) -> str:
        if not value.strip():
            raise ValueError("value must be non-empty")
        return value.strip()

    @field_validator("difficulty_reasons")
    @classmethod
    def concrete_difficulty_reasons(cls, value: list[str]) -> list[str]:
        reasons = [reason.strip() for reason in value if isinstance(reason, str) and reason.strip()]
        if not reasons or len(reasons) != len(value):
            raise ValueError("difficulty_reasons must contain non-empty strings")
        return reasons

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def unique_paths(self) -> "TaskInfo":
        data_paths = [item.path for item in self.data]
        deliverables = [item.path for item in self.required_deliverables]
        if len(data_paths) != len(set(data_paths)):
            raise ValueError("data paths must be unique")
        if not deliverables or len(deliverables) != len(set(deliverables)):
            raise ValueError("required deliverables must be non-empty and unique")
        return self


class ManifestEntry(StrictModel):
    path: str
    size: int = Field(ge=0)
    sha256: str
    visibility: Literal["agent", "metadata", "evaluator"]

    @field_validator("path")
    @classmethod
    def valid_path(cls, value: str) -> str:
        return _safe_path(value)

    @field_validator("sha256")
    @classmethod
    def valid_hash(cls, value: str) -> str:
        if not re.fullmatch(r"[0-9a-f]{64}", value):

Hypsochromic shift of the longwave band absorption maxima in 
DMF compared with ones in the less polar CHCl3 (Table 2) indicate the 
existence of intermolecular hydrogen bonding between the dye mole­
cules and DMF that leads to stabilization of the ground state and 
increasing of energy transition. Exception is observed for 6d and 7d 
which demonstrate bathochromic shift at transition from CHCl3 to DMF. 
It is probably connected with substituent (4-CF3C6H4) which has least 
donor properties compared with other compounds and thus stabilization 
of the excited state is a more preferable. The rarely observed change in 
the position of the absorption maximum in a more polar solvent for 5f,g, 
6a-g, 7a-g is due to CF3 group in the pyrazolone. Thus, for compounds 
8a,b with a methyl substituent, a classic bathochromic shift is observed 
with increasing solvent polarity (Fig. 6a). Fig. 6b shows the absorption 
spectra in CHCl3 and DMF for compound 7a containing the CF3-sub­
stituent in comparison with the non-fluorinated analog 8a.
Fig. S3–S5 and Table 3 show the steady-state fluorescence spectra of 
5f,g, 6a-g, 7a-g in CHCl3 solution. All compounds in CHCl3 solution had 
a weak fluorescence in the range of 520–620 nm with quantum yield 
~0.01. Solid-state emission (Figs. 7 and 8) was also observed for the 
studied compounds with red shifting compared with CHCl3 solution (Δ 
13–108 nm) [44–47]. On the whole quantum yield fluorescence is 
increased in solid state, the most quantum yield is observed for 6c 
(0.07), 6e (0.10) and 7a (0.06). Introduction of electron donating Ar 
(Het) groups (6a-g, 7a-g) leads to red shift emission compared with 5f 
and 5g. Compounds 5f,g, 6a-g, 7a-g exhibit longer fluorescence lifetime 
in the solid state (0.25–1.19 ns) compared with CHCl3 solution 
(0.09–0.94 ns) due to the restriction of intramolecular motion [48]. 
Additionally, the CIE 1931 chromaticity diagrams of compounds 5f,g, 
6a-g, 7a-g are placed into the Supplementary data (Fig. S15–S16).

2.2.2. Antimicrobial activity
The need for new antibiotics is extremely high owing to the wide­
spread resistance of infectious disease pathogens to existing antibacte­
rial drugs. This is especially actual for the bacteria Neisseria gonorrhoeae, 
which has developed resistance to all antimicrobial drugs recommended 
for monotherapy of gonorrhea, including Ceftriaxone [58]. Recently we 
have found among polyfluoroalkyl-containing AHPs the powerful anti­
gonorrheal agents with the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) to 
0.9 μg/mL [35], which was significantly higher than the activity of the 
reference Spectinomycin and was slightly less than that of Ceftriaxone.
In this work, the activity of the synthesized AHPPs 6, 7 was estimated 
in relation to the strain of Neisseria gonorrhoeae ATCC 49226/NCTC 
12700 (CTXS) and, for active compounds, against a clinical isolate 
N. gonorrhoeae 59 (CTXR). As shown in Table 5, from the group of NH- 
pyrazolones 6a-g, compounds 6a-d, f (MIC up to 0.24 μg/mL) have a 
high inhibitory effect against N. gonorrhoeae (CTXS), exceeding the ef­
fect of Spectinomycin by 9–90 times, and the activity of 4-MeS-contain­
ing derivative 6b is at the level of Ceftriaxone. The introduction of a 
phenyl group into the pyrazole core, in general, leads to a decrease in the 
antigonorrheal effect. Pyrazolones 7a-c exceed the activity of Specti­
nomycin by 10–20 times, while compound 7d is the most active in this 
series with an MIC of 0.24 μg/mL. Note that pyrazolone 5g having an 
monoarylhydrazinylidene fragment does not exhibit antigonorrheal 
activity.
For the leading compounds 6a, 6c, 6d, 6f, 7b, 7d, 7f, the inhibitory 
effect against the CTXR strain resistant to Ceftriaxone was evaluated. It 
was found that pyrazolones 6c, 6f, 7b, 7g are not active against this 
strain, whereas compounds 6a, 6d, 7d exhibit high inhibitory properties 
(MIC up to 0.12 μg/mL). The fact that the synthesized pyrazolones 6, 7 
are active against the CTXR strain allowed us to suggest that the 
mechanism of their antibacterial action may be due to interactions with 
other biotargets, which are in not typical for Ceftriaxone.
In addition, the antifungal activity of the compounds against strains 
of three pathogenic dermatophytes (Trichophyton rubrum, Epi­
dermophyton floccosum, Microsporum canis) and one strain of yeast-like 
fungi Candida albicans was evaluated. Fluconazole was used as posi­
tive control (MIC 1.56–3.12 μg/mL). All investigated compounds except 
pyrazolone 6a (MIC 25 μg/mL) did not show activity against C. albicans. 
This compound inhibited the growth of E. floccosum at MIC 12.5 μg/mL. 
Pyrazolone 6g showed weak activity against T. rubrum, E. floccosum 
(MIC 25 μg/mL), and M. canis (MIC 50 μg/mL).

hydrogen bonds with NH-groups of pyrazolone (in seria 6a-g) and

mode NH of hydrazone parts appear as shoulder in case of 6a-g and as

erocycles 6a-g, 7a-g, 8a,b recorded in CDCl3 and DMSO‑d6 contain one 
set of signals, which can also be attributed to the Z-HK tautomer, since 
no change in the chemical shifts of the IHB-associated NNH group pro­
ton signals (δ 12–14 ppm) in the 1H NMR spectra, the signal of the

Results and discussion
Synthesis and characterization
The synthetic routes to the DBC-based compounds DBC-Ph,
DBC-Nap, DBC-Ant, DBC-Pyr, and DBC-Cbz are illustrated in
Scheme 1. The core DBC scaﬀold was obtained in a single step
through the tandem oxidative coupling and cyclization of 2-
naphthylamine (1) under Cu(II)-catalyzed conditions.23 The
resulting DBC intermediate (2) was then subjected to Suzuki
coupling with various arylboronic acids (3), allowing for the
introduction of extended aromatic substituents (DBC-Ph, DBC-
Nap,
DBC-Ant,
and
DBC-Pyr).
The
reactions
proceeded
smoothly under the modied conditions, resulting in the
desired derivatives in moderate to good yield (48–89%). In the
case of DBC-Cbz, the desired product was obtained via the Pd-
catalyzed C–N cross-coupling of (2) with carbazole (4), result-
ing in the corresponding derivative in good yield (88%).
The solid-state structure of DBC-Nap was conrmed through
single-crystal X-ray crystallography (Fig. 2, Tables S1 and S2).
The dihedral angle (C1–N1–C21–C26) between the DBC moiety
and para-substituted phenyl unit was measured as 53.3°, indi-
cating a moderately twisted connection.
Photophysical, electrochemical, and thermal properties
The photophysical properties of DBC-based compounds DBC-
Ph, DBC-Nap, DBC-Ant, DBC-Pyr, and DBC-Cbz, which contain
para-aryl-substituents on the N-phenyl group, were investigated
using UV-vis absorption and PL spectroscopy in oxygen-free
diluted toluene (10 mM) at 298 K (Table 1, Fig. 3a and b). The
absorption spectra all exhibited similar characteristic peaks
(Fig. 3a). The high-energy band at 305–307 nm and low-energy
band at 350 nm correspond to local p–p* and n–p* transi-
tions centered on the DBC moiety, respectively, whereas the
band at 367 nm corresponds to partial intramolecular charge
transfer (ICT) between the DBC moiety and para-substituted N-
phenyl unit, similar to that observed for other DBC deriva-
tives.17,23 Two further absorption peaks were observed at 334
and 387 nm for DBC-Ant, whereas weak shoulder peaks
appeared at approximately 336 and 380 nm for DBC-Pyr. These
features are attributed to the p–p* transitions of the para-
substituted groups (anthracene in DBC-Ant and pyrene in DBC-
Pyr).29,30
The electrochemical properties of the DBC derivatives were
investigated by CV in deoxygenated MeCN (1 mM) and thin lm
(Table 1, Fig. S6 and S7). All compounds underwent irreversible
oxidation in both solution and thin lm. In solution, the
highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energies of DBC-
Cbz, DBC-Nap, DBC-Ant, and DBC-Pyr, as determined from the
oxidation onset potentials, were almost identical at −5.47 eV,
whereas that of DBC-Ph was −5.23 eV. The lowest unoccupied
molecular orbital (LUMO) energies, as calculated from the
HOMO energies and optical bandgaps (Eg), ranged from −1.93
to −2.35 eV for all compounds, with slight variations depending
on the para-aryl-substituent of the N-phenyl group (Table 1).
The thermal stabilities of the DBC-based compounds were
examined using TGA (Table 1 and Fig. 4). The onset of thermal
degradation
(5%
weight
loss
temperature,
Td5)
occurred
between 330 and 438 °C for all compounds, indicating high
thermal stability.
The PL emission spectra of DBC-Ph, DBC-Nap, and DBC-Cbz
exhibited nearly identical broad dual emission peaks within the
range of 374–393 nm (Fig. 3b). These peaks are attributed to the
p–p* transition associated with the DBC moiety, combined
with partial charge transfer (CT) from the DBC moiety to the N-
phenyl unit.23 Additionally, low-energy shoulders and long tails
associated with the ICT appeared at approximately 420 nm and
beyond 470 nm, respectively. The emission wavelengths of these
compounds did not deviate, regardless of the para-substituent
(phenyl, naphthyl, or carbazolyl) on the N-phenyl group.
However, the emission spectra of DBC-Ant and DBC-Pyr diﬀered
signicantly, with broad, structureless bands centered at 406
and 395 nm, respectively. These bands correspond to the p–p*

support their potential as eﬀective chromophores in optoelec-

PAGE 8 compounds described above accumulate primarily in lipid droplets, 
although some of them are also detected in other organelles (in some 
cases, endoplasmic reticulum), although they fluoresce less brightly 
there (Table 4). At the same time, some of pyrazolones penetrates 
through the cell nucleus and binds to DNA in the nucleus, possibly 
binding to RNA-rich regions. All investigated compounds fluoresce 
green under excitation by 405 nm laser, for except pyrazolone 7b, which 
fluoresce yellow. It appears to occur owing to the presence of the SMe 
group in the molecule 7b, which can easily undergo oxidation under 
experimental conditions and cause changes in the fluorescence 
spectrum.
Colocalization tests were performed with commercial dyes to 
confirm the accumulation of the substances under study in lipid droplets 
(Fig. 12). This was not possible with all substances due to the coinci­
dence of their spectra with those of known dyes, but the morphological 
staining patterns of all substances under study are quite similar. The 
Manders coefficient for the colocalization of the substance with the 
nuclear dye was 0.22, for the mitochondrial dye 0.42, and for the lipid 
droplet dye 0.83, which indicates its preferential accumulation in these 
organelles.
2.2.2. Antimicrobial activity
The need for new antibiotics is extremely high owing to the wide­
spread resistance of infectious disease pathogens to existing antibacte­
rial drugs. This is especially actual for the bacteria Neisseria gonorrhoeae, 
which has developed resistance to all antimicrobial drugs recommended 
for monotherapy of gonorrhea, including Ceftriaxone [58]. Recently we 
have found among polyfluoroalkyl-containing AHPs the powerful anti­
gonorrheal agents with the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) to 
0.9 μg/mL [35], which was significantly higher than the activity of the 
reference Spectinomycin and was slightly less than that of Ceftriaxone.
In this work, the activity of the synthesized AHPPs 6, 7 was estimated 
in relation to the strain of Neisseria gonorrhoeae ATCC 49226/NCTC 
12700 (CTXS) and, for active compounds, against a clinical isolate 
N. gonorrhoeae 59 (CTXR). As shown in Table 5, from the group of NH- 
pyrazolones 6a-g, compounds 6a-d, f (MIC up to 0.24 μg/mL) have a 
high inhibitory effect against N. gonorrhoeae (CTXS), exceeding the ef­
fect of Spectinomycin by 9–90 times, and the activity of 4-MeS-contain­
ing derivative 6b is at the level of Ceftriaxone. The introduction of a 
phenyl group into the pyrazole core, in general, leads to a decrease in the 
antigonorrheal effect. Pyrazolones 7a-c exceed the activity of Specti­
nomycin by 10–20 times, while compound 7d is the most active in this 
series with an MIC of 0.24 μg/mL. Note that pyrazolone 5g having an 
monoarylhydrazinylidene fragment does not exhibit antigonorrheal 
activity.
For the leading compounds 6a, 6c, 6d, 6f, 7b, 7d, 7f, the inhibitory 
effect against the CTXR strain resistant to Ceftriaxone was evaluated. It 
was found that pyrazolones 6c, 6f, 7b, 7g are not active against this 
strain, whereas compounds 6a, 6d, 7d exhibit high inhibitory properties 
(MIC up to 0.12 μg/mL). The fact that the synthesized pyrazolones 6, 7 
are active against the CTXR strain allowed us to suggest that the 
mechanism of their antibacterial action may be due to interactions with 
other biotargets, which are in not typical for Ceftriaxone.
In addition, the antifungal activity of the compounds against strains 
of three pathogenic dermatophytes (Trichophyton rubrum, Epi­
dermophyton floccosum, Microsporum canis) and one strain of yeast-like 
fungi Candida albicans was evaluated. Fluconazole was used as posi­
tive control (MIC 1.56–3.12 μg/mL). All investigated compounds except 
pyrazolone 6a (MIC 25 μg/mL) did not show activity against C. albicans. 
This compound inhibited the growth of E. floccosum at MIC 12.5 μg/mL. 
Pyrazolone 6g showed weak activity against T. rubrum, E. floccosum 
(MIC 25 μg/mL), and M. canis (MIC 50 μg/mL).
3. Conclusions
We have proposed a method for the synthesis of 4-biarylhydrazinyli­
denepyrazolones 6a-g, 7a-g, 8a,b by cross-coupling of 4-iodo/bromo­
phenylhydrazinylidenepyrazolones 5a-e with arylboronic acids in the 
presence of K2CO3 and Pd(PPh3)4 catalyst, whereas an alternative 
approach via involvement of 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds in the cross- 
coupling reaction was unsuccessful owing to their cleavage. More
